Name: compression_calibration_drift
Title: Does Compression Break Calibration? A Controlled Study of Quantization and Pruning Effects on Confidence Reliability in Tiny Networks
Short Hypothesis: Post-training quantization and pruning of tiny neural networks systematically shift confidence calibration (typically toward overconfidence) in a way that is predictable from the compression ratio, and a single cheap post-hoc temperature refit after compression is sufficient to restore near-original calibration even though it cannot restore lost accuracy. If true, this decouples 'calibration cost' from 'accuracy cost' of compression and gives a nearly-free recipe for deploying compressed tiny models with reliable confidences.
Related Work: Prior work on calibration of small models studies temperature scaling, label smoothing, ensembles, and mixup in isolation from model compression (as in our own related tiny-model calibration study). Separately, the LLM literature has studied how calibration DATA used during post-training quantization affects downstream task accuracy (Williams & Aletras, 2023), but this is about choosing calibration examples for the compression algorithm itself, not about the calibration (confidence reliability) of the resulting model's predictions -- a completely different sense of 'calibration.' We are not aware of controlled small-scale studies that measure expected calibration error (ECE) as a function of quantization bit-width and pruning sparsity in tiny classifiers, nor of work testing whether a single post-compression temperature refit suffices to correct any induced miscalibration. This distinguishes our proposal from both bodies of work: we study the intersection of model compression and confidence calibration (not calibration data selection for compression, and not calibration methods studied without compression).
Abstract: Efficient on-device inference relies on compressing already-small models via quantization and pruning, but little is known about how these operations affect the reliability of predicted confidences, as distinct from accuracy. We hypothesize that quantization and pruning of tiny neural networks (under one million parameters) induce a predictable calibration drift, generally toward overconfidence as decision boundaries are coarsened by reduced weight precision or sparsified connectivity, and that this drift can be corrected almost for free by refitting a single temperature scalar on a small held-out set after compression, without any retraining. We test this on tiny MLPs and CNNs trained on MNIST, FashionMNIST, and UCI tabular datasets, applying post-training quantization (int8, int4, int2 weights) and unstructured magnitude pruning (30-90% sparsity) across a grid of compression levels. For each configuration we measure expected calibration error (ECE), Brier score, and accuracy before and after a post-compression temperature refit, and we track whether the optimal temperature scales monotonically with compression ratio (allowing prediction of the right temperature from compression level alone, without a validation set). We further test whether calibration drift and its correctability persist under distribution shift (image corruptions, label noise) and whether label smoothing or mixup during original training makes models more robust to compression-induced miscalibration. The result is a controlled empirical map of calibration cost as a function of compression, plus a practical, near-zero-cost recipe (refit-temperature-after-compression) for deploying compressed tiny models with trustworthy confidence estimates, all runnable in minutes on CPU or a single small GPU.
Experiments: (1) Train baseline tiny models: 2-3 layer MLPs (<100K params) on UCI tabular tasks (e.g. Adult, Covertype subsample) and small CNNs (<1M params) on MNIST/FashionMNIST, subsampled to <=10K training examples, with standard cross-entropy loss. (2) Apply post-training quantization to weights (and optionally activations) at int8, int4, int2 precision using simple uniform quantization (no need for advanced PTQ libraries -- implement min-max quantization manually). (3) Apply unstructured magnitude pruning at sparsity levels {30%,50%,70%,90%} with one-shot fine-tuning-free pruning. (4) For each of the resulting ~20-30 (quantization x pruning) configurations, measure test accuracy, ECE (15-bin), Brier score, and reliability diagrams both before and after refitting a single temperature scalar (fit by minimizing NLL on a small held-out calibration split of 500-1000 examples). (5) Test the 'monotonic temperature' hypothesis: regress optimal post-compression temperature against a simple scalar compression metric (e.g., bits-per-weight x (1-sparsity)) and report R^2; if strong, this supports predicting temperature without a calibration set. (6) Repeat under distribution shift: corrupt test images (Gaussian noise, blur, brightness at 3 severities) and inject symmetric label noise (5%, 10%) into a fraction of training data, re-measuring whether the pre-compression temperature-refit recipe still restores calibration post-shift, or whether shift and compression interact non-additively. (7) Ablation: repeat the full pipeline for models originally trained with label smoothing (alpha=0.1) or mixup, testing whether these training-time interventions make models more robust to compression-induced miscalibration (smaller drift, smaller temperature correction needed). (8) Report all results as heatmaps of ECE over the (bit-width, sparsity) grid, before/after refit, plus the temperature-vs-compression regression fit.
Risk Factors and Limitations: Unstructured pruning at high sparsity without fine-tuning may collapse accuracy so much that calibration metrics become uninformative (need to report accuracy alongside ECE and possibly exclude degenerate configurations). Simple manual quantization may not reflect real deployed quantization kernels (e.g., per-channel quantization, activation quantization nuances); results may not transfer directly to production quantization toolchains. The 'monotonic temperature' relationship may not hold cleanly across model architectures or datasets, weakening the practical recipe claim -- this would still be a valid and useful negative result but changes the paper's contribution from a prescriptive recipe to a diagnostic map. Single temperature scaling only corrects global miscalibration and may fail to capture class-conditional or subgroup miscalibration introduced by compression, which the study does not directly address unless extended with class-wise ECE. Findings from MNIST/FashionMNIST/UCI-scale tasks may not generalize to more complex data distributions.

Name: calibration_double_descent
Title: Miscalibration at the Interpolation Threshold: Can Cheap Calibration Fixes Tame the Double-Descent Confidence Spike?
Short Hypothesis: As tiny classifiers are swept from under- to over-parameterized (fixed data, increasing width), expected calibration error exhibits its own spike right at the interpolation threshold that is sharper and more transient than the accompanying test-error double descent, and this spike is attenuated by training-time interventions (label smoothing, small ensembles) but not by post-hoc temperature scaling, which only rescales an already-unstable decision boundary. Tiny models with an explicit, controllable width sweep are the cleanest setting to isolate this effect because the interpolation threshold can be pinpointed exactly and swept densely and cheaply.
Related Work: Nakkiran et al. (2019, 'Deep Double Descent') show test error and test loss can behave non-monotonically in model size and training epochs, and note in passing that test loss double-descents even when test accuracy does not, which implicitly reflects confidence miscalibration but is never measured as ECE or studied as a calibration phenomenon. Rahaman & Thiery (NeurIPS 2020) study uncertainty quantification and deep ensembles under overparameterization and observe that NLL/calibration-related quantities can degrade near the interpolation threshold, but they do not compare the standard cheap calibration toolkit (temperature scaling vs. label smoothing vs. ensembling) as targeted fixes for this specific regime, nor do they characterize the spike's width/location as a function of label noise in a controlled, dense width sweep. Our own related tiny-model calibration study asks which cheap interventions help in a generic (non-double-descent) setting; this proposal instead asks whether the *ranking* of those same interventions flips specifically at the interpolation threshold, a regime-dependent question not addressed by either literature. This is a genuinely different question from prior double descent papers (which document the phenomenon) and from generic calibration papers (which don't consider model-capacity regime as a variable): we test whether known cheap fixes are differentially effective exactly where calibration is worst.
Abstract: Double descent shows that test loss and error can behave non-monotonically as model capacity crosses the interpolation threshold, but whether *confidence calibration* specifically spikes at this threshold, and whether standard cheap calibration interventions can suppress that spike, remains unexamined. We hypothesize that expected calibration error (ECE) exhibits a sharp, localized peak at the interpolation threshold that is not simply explained by the co-occurring test-accuracy peak, and that this miscalibration spike is preferentially fixed by training-time interventions (label smoothing, small deep ensembles of 3-4 members) rather than by post-hoc temperature scaling, because temperature scaling can only rescale probabilities and cannot correct the instability of decision boundaries fit to a near-perfectly-memorized, noisy training set. We test this using tiny MLPs (width swept from 1 to 4096 hidden units) on subsampled MNIST/FashionMNIST and UCI tabular tasks with injected label noise (0%, 10%, 20%) to reliably induce a clean double-descent curve, densely sampling width near the known interpolation threshold. For each width and noise level we measure train/test accuracy, ECE, NLL, and Brier score with and without each calibration intervention, averaged over multiple seeds. We quantify the calibration spike as excess ECE relative to a smooth baseline fit away from the threshold, and test whether label smoothing and ensembling significantly reduce spike magnitude relative to temperature scaling, while all methods perform comparably in the classical under- and over-parameterized regimes. The result is a precise, mechanistic map of where and why cheap calibration fixes succeed or fail as a function of model capacity relative to data, directly actionable for practitioners deciding which model size and calibration method to deploy together.
Experiments: (1) Establish a clean double-descent setting: tiny MLPs (1 hidden layer, width in {1,2,4,...,4096}, ~40 widths) trained on MNIST subsampled to 4,000 examples with symmetric label noise at {0%, 10%, 20%}, following Nakkiran-style setup, trained to convergence with fixed epochs/optimizer across all widths, 5 seeds per width. (2) For each (width, noise, seed), record train/test accuracy, test NLL, 15-bin ECE, and Brier score; locate the interpolation threshold as the width where train accuracy first reaches ~100%. (3) Fit a baseline calibration-vs-width curve using local regression on the under- and over-parameterized regions (excluding a window around the threshold) and define 'spike magnitude' as the max excess ECE inside that window relative to the fitted baseline. (4) Repeat steps 1-3 with three interventions applied at/after training: (a) post-hoc temperature scaling (fit on a 500-example held-out split), (b) label smoothing (alpha=0.1) during training, (c) 3-member deep ensembles (same architecture, different seeds, averaged softmax). (5) Compare spike magnitude across intervention conditions using paired tests (paired by width/noise across seeds) to test the core hypothesis: label smoothing and ensembling produce significantly smaller spikes than temperature scaling and no-intervention, with no significant difference between methods away from the threshold. (6) Test generalization of the phenomenon: repeat the width sweep with a small CNN (<200K params, varying channel width) on FashionMNIST, and with tiny MLPs on a UCI tabular dataset (e.g. Adult) with injected label noise, to check whether the spike-and-fix pattern replicates across modalities. (7) Secondary check: repeat with an epoch-wise (rather than model-size) double descent sweep at fixed large width, training for many epochs and tracking calibration vs. epoch, to see if the same intervention ranking holds along the temporal axis. (8) Report calibration-vs-width curves (with confidence bands) for each intervention and noise level, plus a summary table of spike magnitude reduction per method, and a decision-rule figure recommending which calibration method to use as a function of estimated proximity to the interpolation threshold.
Risk Factors and Limitations: The double-descent peak in small models can be narrow and seed-sensitive, so a dense width grid and multiple seeds (5+) are needed to reliably localize and measure it, adding compute though still feasible on CPU/small GPU given tiny model sizes. Defining 'spike magnitude' via a local-regression baseline is somewhat arbitrary and results should be checked for robustness to the choice of window size and smoothing method. If test accuracy itself has no visible double descent for a given dataset/noise level (some settings show only monotonic curves), the calibration-spike hypothesis cannot be tested there, so careful pre-validation of a clean accuracy double descent curve is required (following established recipes with label noise, as in Nakkiran et al.) before running the calibration analysis. The mechanistic explanation (decision-boundary instability under-served by temperature rescaling) is plausible but not the only possible explanation, so the paper should present it as an empirically supported hypothesis rather than a proven mechanism, potentially supplemented with a small diagnostic (e.g., variance of predictions across seeds/bootstraps near the threshold) to partially probe the mechanism. Findings from MNIST/FashionMNIST/UCI-scale tiny models may not transfer to large-scale double descent regimes (e.g., transformer scaling), which is out of scope but should be noted as a limitation.
